bibliographic.title: Valuing On-the-Ball Actions in Soccer: A Critical Comparison of xT and VAEP
bibliographic.venue: AAAI-20 Workshop on Artificial Intelligence in Team Sports

scope.rationale: Critical conceptual and empirical comparison of two canonical action-valuation frameworks (xT and VAEP). The paper proposes no new method, but analyses design-choice differences, computes both rankings on StatsBomb Premier League 2018/2019 data, and contrasts the two methods on illustrative action types, top-25 player rankings, correlation with goals/assists, and split-half robustness.

model.name: xT vs VAEP (critical comparison)
inputs: ball location (zone on M x N pitch grid) for xT
previous three actions including action type, start/end location, distance and angle to goal for VAEP
action-context features such as distance covered and time elapsed between consecutive actions for VAEP
game-context features such as time remaining in the match and current score differential for VAEP
model.target: For xT: probability of scoring within the next i actions (zone value). For VAEP: P_score and P_concede within the next k actions, action value = delta P_score - delta P_concede.
model.architecture: xT: closed-form Markov chain solved iteratively over an M x N grid (16 x 12 in this paper, converged after 6 iterations). VAEP: two separate XGBoost gradient boosted tree classifiers (one for P_score, one for P_concede) trained on a feature representation of the last three actions plus game context.
model.spatial_resolution: 16 x 12 pitch grid (xT); continuous location features (VAEP)
model.temporal_horizon: xT: probability of scoring within the next i actions (iteratively expanded until convergence). VAEP: next k actions (fixed-length action window).

metrics: Jaccard similarity coefficient between top-k rankings
Pearson correlation with goals per 90 minutes (g/90)
Pearson correlation with assists per 90 minutes (a/90)
Pearson correlation between split-half player ratings (robustness)
evaluation.splits: Models trained on StatsBomb English Premier League 2017/2018 season and used to rate actions in the 2018/2019 season. Robustness analysis splits the data into two random disjoint subsets and computes Pearson correlation of per-player ratings across them.

claims.statement: xT and VAEP produce different top-25 player rankings; their top-25 rankings have a Jaccard similarity coefficient of 0.48.
claims.evidence_location: Section 'Comparison of top-25 player rankings'; Figure 3; Table 1

claims.statement: After the top 25 players, the Jaccard similarity coefficient between xT and VAEP rankings drops to 0.35 before steadily increasing.
claims.evidence_location: Section 'Comparison of top-25 player rankings'; Figure 3

claims.statement: VAEP correlates more strongly with goals per 90 minutes than xT (rho_g/90 = 0.41 for VAEP vs 0.26 for xT).
xT correlates more strongly with assists per 90 minutes than VAEP (rho_a/90 = 0.53 for xT vs 0.33 for VAEP).
xT ratings are more robust across two random disjoint subsets of the season than VAEP ratings (Pearson rho = 0.89 for xT vs rho = 0.25 for VAEP).
When restricted to offensive values of passes, dribbles and crosses (the actions xT can value), VAEP's split-half robustness improves to rho = 0.59.
Top-25 xT player ranking for 2018/2019 Premier League is led by Eden Hazard (rating 0.547, g/90 = 0.49, a/90 = 0.46); top-25 VAEP ranking is also led by Eden Hazard (rating 0.558).
Virgil van Dijk, a top-class defender, is ranked 81st by VAEP and 142nd by xT, illustrating that both rankings favour attacking players.
Sergio Aguero is ranked 19th by VAEP but absent from xT's top 25, attributed to VAEP rewarding his overperformance on shots (finishing skill).
Alexis Sanchez is ranked 7th by xT but absent from VAEP's top 25, attributed to xT crediting his key passes into high-value zones even though his shot volume halved.
xT cannot value actions that do not move the ball between zones (e.g., short dribbles inside the penalty box, take-ons within the same zone) and assigns them a value of zero by definition.
claims.evidence_location: Section 'xT can only value ball-progressing actions' and footnote 4; Figure 2c

claims.statement: Backward passes into the own penalty box occur roughly 19 times per game; xT does not capture their risk/reward whereas VAEP assigns more diverse positive and negative values.
claims.evidence_location: Section 'Backward passes into a team's own penalty box'; Figure 2a

claims.statement: First ball progressions of counter attacks occur roughly 2 to 3 times per game; VAEP's value distribution has higher mean and variance, while xT values are extremely skewed towards zero.
claims.evidence_location: Section 'First ball progression of counter attacks'; Figure 2b

claims.statement: Successful forward dribbles inside the penalty box occur roughly four times per game; xT assigns zero to a major part of them because they do not change zone.
claims.evidence_location: Section 'Forward dribbles inside the penalty box'; Figure 2c

claims.statement: Completed forward passes to within 3 metres of the penalty-box border occur roughly 5 times per game; xT, on average, values such through balls higher than VAEP does.
claims.evidence_location: Section 'Completed forward passes to the border of the penalty box'; Figure 2d

claims.statement: The xT model in this paper uses a 16 x 12 grid and reaches convergence after 6 iterations; the VAEP model uses XGBoost.
Both xT and VAEP rankings deviate from traditional metrics such as goals or assists per 90 minutes, suggesting they provide additional insight into player performance.
claims.evidence_location: Abstract; Conclusion; Section 'Comparison with traditional performance metrics'

limitations: Determining the ground truth of action values is very difficult, if not impossible; deciding which of xT and VAEP gives the better estimate for specific action types is not straightforward.
Both rankings are biased towards attacking players because offensive actions have access to higher rewards in both frameworks, so defensive players are ranked much lower.
VAEP's detailed feature-based representation comes at a cost in interpretability: explaining why a particular value is assigned to a specific game state is no longer straightforward.

Because VAEP assigns goals high action values, aggregated player ratings can vary significantly based on whether a small number of goals are included; for defensive players a difference of only three goals can double or halve their ratings.
